title: Organic formulas, functional groups and homologous series
summary: An organic molecule can be written several ways, from a [[molecular-formula|molecular formula]] to a [[skeletal-formula|skeletal formula]], and you need to switch between them. A [[functional-group|functional group]] decides how a compound behaves. Compounds with the same group form a [[homologous-series|homologous series]]: one general formula, and boiling points that rise steadily along it.

goals.text: Recognise empirical, molecular, structural, skeletal and stereochemical formulas, and convert between molecular, structural and skeletal formulas.
Name and recognise the nine functional groups the course lists, and decide whether a compound is [[saturated|saturated]] or [[unsaturated|unsaturated]].
Place a compound in its homologous series and use general formulas to find molecular formulas.
Describe and explain how boiling and melting points change along a series, and how branching and the functional group change them.

before.prompt: Hex-1-ene has the molecular formula $\ce{C6H12}$. What is its [[empirical-formula|empirical formula]]?
before.hint: Divide both numbers by the largest number that goes into both.
before.explain: 6 and 12 share a factor of 6, so the simplest ratio is $\ce{CH2}$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.7}}.

before.prompt: Pentane, $\ce{C5H12}$, boils at $36\,^{\circ}\text{C}$. What is overcome when it boils?
before.hint: Do the pentane molecules themselves change when the liquid turns to gas?
before.explain: Boiling separates whole molecules, so only [[intermolecular-force|intermolecular forces]] are overcome: in non-polar pentane, [[london-dispersion-force|London (dispersion) forces]]. Revise it in {{lesson:2.6}}.

before.prompt: How many [[covalent-bond|covalent bonds]] does a carbon atom form in a neutral molecule such as methane or ethanol?
before.hint: Carbon has four outer electrons and needs eight in its outer shell.
before.explain: Carbon shares its four outer electrons in four bonds to reach an octet; a double bond counts as two. Revise it in {{lesson:2.2}}.

blocks.text: Carbon forms four [[covalent-bond|covalent bonds]] and bonds strongly to itself, so it builds chains, branches and rings of almost any size. Each kind of formula shows a different amount of detail.
1. Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Ethane, $\ce{C2H6}$, has the empirical formula $\ce{CH3}$.
2. Molecular formula: the actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule, such as $\ce{C3H8O}$.
3. [[structural-formula|Structural formula]]: shows which atom is bonded to which. A full one draws every bond; a condensed one groups the atoms on each carbon: $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$.
4. [[skeletal-formula|Skeletal formula]]: a zig-zag line drawing. Every corner and line end is a carbon, and hydrogens on carbon are left out. Other atoms, and any H on them, are written in.
5. Stereochemical formula: shows the 3D shape with wedges (towards you) and dashes (away). Recognise one; draw one only when asked.

blocks.alt: Propan-1-ol shown five ways. Top left, the full structural formula: three carbon atoms in a row, each with a hydrogen above and below, a fourth hydrogen on the left-hand carbon, and the right-hand carbon bonded to an oxygen, which is bonded to a hydrogen. Top right, the condensed structural formula CH3CH2CH2OH. Bottom left, the skeletal formula: a zig-zag of two lines meeting at a corner, with a third line from the right-hand end to OH. Bottom right, the stereochemical formula: the same chain, with each carbon's hydrogens drawn as one solid wedge and one dashed wedge, and an extra hydrogen in the plane on the end carbon. Below: molecular formula C3H8O and empirical formula C3H8O.
blocks.caption: Propan-1-ol. Its empirical and molecular formulas match, because 3, 8 and 1 share no common factor.

blocks.statement: To turn a skeletal formula into a molecular formula, count a carbon at every corner and line end, give each carbon enough H for four bonds, then add the atoms written in.
blocks.why: In a neutral molecule carbon always forms four bonds, so every bond left out is a $\ce{C-H}$ bond.

blocks.question: Pentan-3-one has the condensed structural formula $\ce{CH3CH2COCH2CH3}$. Deduce its molecular formula.
steps: Read the groups from left to right: $\ce{CH3}$, $\ce{CH2}$, $\ce{CO}$, $\ce{CH2}$, $\ce{CH3}$.
Carbon: one in each group, so 5.
Oxygen: one, in the $\ce{CO}$ group. Write C first, then H, then the other elements.

blocks.alt: Skeletal formula: an HO group on the left joined to a zig-zag chain of four carbon atoms, with a one-carbon branch pointing down from the third carbon of the chain.
blocks.caption: 3-methylbutan-1-ol, which smells of bananas.

blocks.question: Deduce the molecular formula of 3-methylbutan-1-ol from the skeletal formula above.
steps: Carbons: four in the zig-zag chain plus one at the end of the branch, so 5.
H on each carbon makes four bonds: the two chain $\ce{CH2}$ carbons have 2 each, the branch point has 1, and the two line ends have 3 each.
H: $2 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 3 = 11$ on carbon, plus 1 in $\ce{OH}$, so 12. One O.

blocks.text: Forgetting the hydrogen on an O or N atom. A skeletal formula hides only the hydrogens on carbon, so the $\ce{OH}$ hydrogen still counts.
In a full structural formula, check every connection: a carbon bonded to the H of an $\ce{OH}$, instead of to the O, loses the mark.

blocks.hint: Does it show how the atoms are joined, carbon by carbon?
blocks.explain: It lists the atoms on each carbon in order, with the $\ce{OH}$ on the second carbon of the chain (butan-2-ol). Its molecular formula is $\ce{C4H10O}$.

blocks.prompt: Butane-1,4-diol, $\ce{HOCH2CH2CH2CH2OH}$, is used to make plastics. What is its empirical formula?
blocks.hint: Find the molecular formula first, then look for a common factor.
blocks.explain: It is $\ce{C4H10O2}$ (count the two $\ce{OH}$ hydrogens). Dividing by 2 gives $\ce{C2H5O}$.

blocks.text: Most of an organic molecule is an unreactive chain of carbon and hydrogen. The reactive part is usually small: a $\ce{C=C}$, or a group containing O, N or a halogen.

blocks.statement: An atom or group of atoms in a molecule that gives the compound its characteristic chemical reactions and strongly affects its physical properties.
blocks.plain: The part of the molecule that decides how it behaves.

blocks.text: A [[functional-group|functional group]] reacts in much the same way on any chain, so compounds are sorted into classes by their groups.
Learn the nine groups below by name and structure, and the class each makes. Questions ask for one or the other.

blocks.alt: Table of functional groups with their structures and the class of compound each gives. Alkenyl, C=C, in alkenes. Alkynyl, C triple bond C, in alkynes. Halogeno, a halogen atom X equal to F, Cl, Br or I, in halogenoalkanes. Hydroxyl, OH, in alcohols. Carbonyl, either CHO at the end of a chain or CO between two carbons, in aldehydes or ketones. Carboxyl, COOH, in carboxylic acids. Alkoxy, O bonded to a carbon chain R, in ethers. Amino, NH2, in amines. Amido, CONH2 or CONH, in amides. Ester, COO, in esters. Phenyl, C6H5, in aromatic compounds.
blocks.caption: [[alkene|Alkenes]] and [[alkyne|alkynes]] are listed too: their $\ce{C=C}$ and $\ce{C#C}$ bonds are what react.

blocks.text: The [[hydroxyl-group|hydroxyl group]], $\ce{-OH}$, is covalently bonded to carbon. It is not the hydroxide ion, $\ce{OH-}$, so [[alcohol|alcohols]] are not bases.

The [[carbonyl-group|carbonyl group]] is $\ce{C=O}$. At the end of a chain, written $\ce{-CHO}$, it makes an [[aldehyde|aldehyde]]. Inside the chain, with a carbon on each side, it makes a [[ketone|ketone]].
The [[carboxyl-group|carboxyl group]], $\ce{-COOH}$, has $\ce{C=O}$ and $\ce{O-H}$ on one carbon. It is one group, not a carbonyl plus a hydroxyl, and it makes a [[carboxylic-acid|carboxylic acid]].
A [[halogeno-group|halogeno group]] is a halogen bonded to carbon, as in the [[halogenoalkane|halogenoalkanes]]. Phenyl, $\ce{-C6H5}$, is a benzene ring, drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside.

Two pairs look alike. Amino, $\ce{-NH2}$, makes an [[amine|amine]]; amido, $\ce{-CONH2}$, has the N on a $\ce{C=O}$ carbon. Alkoxy is an O between two carbons; an ester, $\ce{-COO-}$, also has a $\ce{C=O}$ beside that O.

A compound with only single bonds between its carbon atoms is [[saturated|saturated]]. One with at least one $\ce{C=C}$ or $\ce{C#C}$ bond is [[unsaturated|unsaturated]]: other atoms can add across the multiple bond.

blocks.alt: Skeletal formula of paracetamol: a benzene ring drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. An OH group is bonded to the top of the ring. An NH group is bonded to the bottom of the ring. The N is also bonded to a carbon that has a double bond to an oxygen atom and a single bond to a line end, a methyl group.
blocks.caption: Paracetamol, a common painkiller.

blocks.question: Identify the three functional groups in paracetamol, shown above.
steps: The hexagon with a circle is a benzene ring: a phenyl group.
The $\ce{OH}$ is covalently bonded to the ring: hydroxyl, not hydroxide.
The N sits next to a $\ce{C=O}$, so the whole unit is amido. It is not amino, and the $\ce{C=O}$ is not a separate ketone.
blocks.answer: Paracetamol contains a hydroxyl group, $\ce{-OH}$. It contains an amido group, $\ce{-NHCO-}$. It contains a phenyl group, the benzene ring.

blocks.question: Hex-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH2CH2CH3}$, and cyclohexane, a ring of six $\ce{CH2}$ groups, both have the molecular formula $\ce{C6H12}$. Deduce, giving a reason, which of them is unsaturated.
steps: The same molecular formula hides different structures, so look at the bonds.
Hex-1-ene has a $\ce{C=C}$.
Cyclohexane closes into a ring and has only single carbon–carbon bonds.
blocks.answer: Hex-1-ene is unsaturated because it contains a carbon–carbon double bond. Cyclohexane is saturated because it has only single bonds between its carbon atoms, which form a ring.

verify.truth: hex-1-ene has a C=C; cyclohexane has only single C-C bonds in a ring

blocks.text: Asked for the functional group? Give the group (carbonyl). Asked for the class or series? Give the class (ketone).

blocks.prompt: A molecule contains the group $\ce{-CONH2}$. Which functional group is this?
blocks.hint: Look at what the nitrogen is bonded to.
blocks.explain: The N is on a carbon that also carries $\ce{=O}$, so it is amido. Amino is $\ce{-NH2}$ on a carbon with no $\ce{C=O}$, and carboxyl is $\ce{-COOH}$.

blocks.prompt: Propan-2-ol is $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH3}$. What is the name of its functional group?
blocks.hint: The $\ce{OH}$ is covalently bonded to carbon.
blocks.explain: A covalently bonded $\ce{-OH}$ is hydroxyl. Hydroxide is the ion $\ce{OH-}$, alkoxy is O between two carbons, and carboxyl needs a $\ce{C=O}$ too.

blocks.text: Methanol, ethanol and propan-1-ol are like the rungs of a ladder. Each has one $\ce{OH}$ group, and each is one $\ce{CH2}$ unit longer than the one before.

blocks.statement: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each member one $\ce{CH2}$ unit longer than the last.
blocks.plain: A ladder of similar molecules, one $\ce{CH2}$ apart.

blocks.text: Members of a [[homologous-series|homologous series]] share a functional group, so they react alike. Physical properties such as boiling point change gradually along it.

The simplest series is the [[alkane|alkanes]]: saturated hydrocarbons. Open-chain alkanes are $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$, where $n$ is the number of carbon atoms; closing a ring, as in cyclohexane, removes two hydrogens. Methane is $\ce{CH4}$ and ethane is $\ce{C2H6}$.
A $\ce{C=C}$ bond removes two hydrogens, giving the [[alkene|alkenes]], $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}}$. A $\ce{C#C}$ bond removes four, giving the [[alkyne|alkynes]], $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n-2}}$.
Other series swap a group into an alkane. A halogenoalkane replaces one H by a halogen, $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+1}X}$; an alcohol puts O between a C and an H, $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+1}OH}$.

blocks.alt: Table of twelve homologous series with general formula and first member, where n is the number of carbon atoms. Alkanes, CnH2n+2, methane CH4. Alkenes, CnH2n, ethene C2H4. Alkynes, CnH2n minus 2, ethyne C2H2. Halogenoalkanes, CnH2n+1X, chloromethane CH3Cl. Alcohols, CnH2n+1OH, methanol CH3OH. Aldehydes, CnH2nO, methanal HCHO. Ketones, CnH2nO, propanone CH3COCH3. Carboxylic acids, CnH2nO2, methanoic acid HCOOH. Ethers, CnH2n+2O, methoxymethane CH3OCH3. Amines, CnH2n+3N, methanamine CH3NH2. Amides, CnH2n+1NO, methanamide HCONH2. Esters, CnH2nO2, methyl methanoate HCOOCH3.
blocks.caption: The twelve series in the course, for open-chain members with one functional group.

blocks.text: Some series share a general formula: aldehydes and ketones are both $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}O}$, acids and esters both $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}O2}$. Only a structural formula tells them apart ({{lesson:3.7}}).
A series starts with its smallest possible molecule: one carbon for alkanes, alcohols and acids; two for alkenes, alkynes, ethers and esters; three for ketones.

blocks.question: Deduce the molecular formula of the fifth member of the alcohols.
steps: The first alcohol is methanol, with one carbon, so the fifth has $n = 5$.
Check: each step up the series adds $\ce{CH2}$. Methanol is $\ce{CH3OH}$; four more $\ce{CH2}$ units give $\ce{C5H11OH}$.

blocks.question: Butanoic acid, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COOH}$, and pentanoic acid, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2COOH}$, are in the same homologous series. Outline three features that show this.
steps: Compare the functional groups: both end in $\ce{-COOH}$.
Compare the formulas: pentanoic acid has one more $\ce{CH2}$.
Test a general formula: $\ce{C4H8O2}$ and $\ce{C5H10O2}$ both fit $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}O2}$.
blocks.answer: Both contain the same functional group, the carboxyl group. They differ by one $\ce{CH2}$ unit. Both fit the same general formula, $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}O2}$, with $n = 4$ and $n = 5$.

verify.truth: same functional group (carboxyl), differ by CH2, same general formula

blocks.text: Counting members from the wrong start. The first alkene is ethene, $\ce{C2H4}$, because a $\ce{C=C}$ needs two carbons. So the third alkene has four carbons, not three.

blocks.prompt: An alkane molecule has 16 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have?
blocks.hint: Use the general formula of the alkanes.
blocks.explain: $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$ with $n = 16$ gives $2(16) + 2 = 34$, so the formula is $\ce{C16H34}$.

blocks.prompt: What is the molecular formula of an alkyne with seven carbon atoms?
blocks.hint: A triple bond takes away four hydrogens compared with the alkane.
blocks.explain: $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n-2}}$ with $n = 7$ gives $14 - 2 = 12$. $\ce{C7H14}$ is an alkene and $\ce{C7H16}$ is the alkane.

sections.heading: Trends in boiling and melting points

blocks.text: Each extra $\ce{CH2}$ adds eight electrons and lengthens the molecule. The functional group stays the same, so the main change is in the [[london-dispersion-force|London (dispersion) forces]].
More electrons give a cloud that distorts more easily, and a longer chain has more surface contact with its neighbours. Both strengthen London forces.

blocks.statement: Along a homologous series, boiling points rise as the chain gets longer. Melting points generally rise too, less smoothly.
blocks.why: Each extra $\ce{CH2}$ strengthens the London forces. Melting also depends on how the molecules pack, so its trend is less regular.

blocks.alt: Graph of boiling point in degrees Celsius against number of carbon atoms, 1 to 6, for straight-chain alkanes and alcohols. Alkanes: minus 162, minus 89, minus 42, minus 1, 36 and 69. Alcohols with the OH on the end carbon: 65, 78, 97, 118, 138 and 157. Both lines rise steadily, and the alcohol line lies well above the alkane line throughout. A dashed line marks 25 degrees Celsius: the first four alkanes lie below it and are gases at room temperature, while every alcohol shown lies above it.
blocks.caption: Both rise with chain length. The alcohols are higher because they also form [[hydrogen-bond|hydrogen bonds]].

blocks.text: So the first four straight-chain alkanes are gases at room temperature, the next are liquids, and long ones are waxy solids. Fractional [[distillation|distillation]] of crude oil uses this trend.

Branching lowers the boiling point: compact molecules touch over less area, so London forces are weaker. Pentane boils at $36\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane at $10\,^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The functional group can add stronger [[intermolecular-force|intermolecular forces]]: $\ce{OH}$ allows hydrogen bonding, and $\ce{C=O}$ adds [[dipole-dipole-force|dipole–dipole forces]].

blocks.question: Explain why octane, $\ce{C8H18}$, has a higher boiling point than hexane, $\ce{C6H14}$.
steps: Name the forces: both are non-polar, so London forces only.
Compare: octane has two more $\ce{CH2}$ units, so more electrons and a longer chain.
Link stronger forces to more energy.
blocks.answer: Both are non-polar alkanes, so only London (dispersion) forces act between their molecules. Octane molecules have more electrons and a longer chain, giving more surface contact. So the London forces between octane molecules are stronger, and more energy is needed to overcome them.

verify.truth: more electrons and surface contact give stronger London forces, needing more energy to overcome

blocks.question: Propan-1-ol, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$, boils at $97\,^{\circ}\text{C}$. Butane, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH3}$, boils at $-1\,^{\circ}\text{C}$. Both molecules have 34 electrons. Explain the difference in boiling points.
steps: Same electrons, so similar London forces: they can't explain a gap of nearly $100\,^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Propan-1-ol has H on O, so it hydrogen bonds. Butane has no H on N, O or F.
Link the stronger forces to more energy.
blocks.answer: Both molecules have the same number of electrons, so their London forces are similar. Propan-1-ol has a hydroxyl group, so its molecules also form hydrogen bonds. Butane has no H on N, O or F, so it has only London forces. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger, so more energy is needed to separate propan-1-ol molecules.

verify.truth: similar London forces; propan-1-ol also hydrogen bonds, which are stronger, so more energy is needed

blocks.text: Explaining a higher boiling point by "more bonds to break". Boiling a molecular liquid only overcomes the forces between molecules; the molecules stay intact.

blocks.prompt: Which isomer of $\ce{C6H14}$ has the highest boiling point?
blocks.hint: Which shape gives the most contact between neighbouring molecules?
blocks.explain: All four have the same electrons. Unbranched hexane has the most surface contact, so the strongest London forces; more branching means a lower boiling point.

blocks.prompt: Why do boiling points rise from propane to butane to pentane?
blocks.hint: What kind of force acts between alkane molecules, and what makes it stronger?

options.text: London forces get stronger as the molecules gain electrons and surface area.
More covalent bonds must be broken in longer molecules.
Hydrogen bonding gets stronger as the chain gets longer.
Longer alkane molecules are more polar.

blocks.explain: Alkanes are non-polar and cannot hydrogen bond, and boiling breaks no covalent bonds. Each extra $\ce{CH2}$ adds electrons and surface contact, so the London forces grow.

verify.truth: London forces get stronger as the molecules gain electrons and surface area.

blocks.text: Formulas: empirical (simplest ratio), molecular (actual atoms), structural (full or condensed), skeletal (C at corners, H on C omitted), stereochemical (wedges).

Functional groups: hydroxyl $\ce{-OH}$, carbonyl $\ce{C=O}$, carboxyl $\ce{-COOH}$, halogeno $\ce{-X}$, amino $\ce{-NH2}$, amido $\ce{-CONH2}$, alkoxy $\ce{-O-R}$, ester $\ce{-COO-}$, phenyl $\ce{-C6H5}$.
Saturated: only single bonds between carbon atoms. Unsaturated: at least one $\ce{C=C}$ or $\ce{C#C}$.
A homologous series shares one functional group and one general formula; neighbouring members differ by $\ce{CH2}$.

General formulas (open chains, one functional group): alkanes $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}$, alkenes $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}}$, alkynes $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n-2}}$, alcohols $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n+1}OH}$, carboxylic acids $\ce{C_{n}H_{2n}O2}$.
Boiling point rises with chain length along a series and falls with branching among isomers. At similar molar mass, hydrogen-bonding groups such as $\ce{-OH}$ raise it.

mistakes: Writing "hydroxide" for an alcohol's $\ce{-OH}$. It is a hydroxyl group, covalently bonded to carbon.
Calling a $\ce{C=O}$ inside a chain an aldehyde. It is a carbonyl group in a ketone; aldehydes have it at the chain end.
Mixing up amino ($\ce{-NH2}$) and amido ($\ce{-CONH2}$, N on a $\ce{C=O}$ carbon).
Saying covalent bonds break when an alkane boils. Only the forces between molecules are overcome.
examTips: "Identify" a functional group: give its name, such as hydroxyl, and its class only if asked.
"Deduce" a molecular formula from a skeletal one: count C, then H on carbon, then other atoms with their H.
"Explain" a boiling point difference: name the forces in each, say which are stronger and why, then link to the energy needed.
